1.stem: Which of the following best describes what the narrator of Passage B says he saw "a great deal more of" than sadness at his laundromat?

options.A: children being taught household skills he himself had mastered.
options.B: small kindnesses between people who did not know one another.
options.C: customers confiding secrets they would never have told a priest.
options.D: arguments between strangers that ended without any resolution.

2.stem: According to the passage, most of the work that comes through the shop door involves:

options.A: replacing the batteries in customers' wristwatches.
options.B: ordering replacement parts from a catalog.
options.C: regulating watches on the timing stand.
options.D: fitting hairsprings into pocket watches.

3.stem: The statement in paragraph 17 that Walter "let it go, which she had not expected" most strongly suggests that:

options.A: in the past Walter would have kept arguing a point until one of them walked out.
options.B: Corinne had expected Walter to admit that the notice was not the reason she came.
options.C: Corinne had hoped Walter would ask her directly why she had come.
options.D: Walter no longer cares whether the building is torn down.

4.stem: It can reasonably be inferred from the description of captive birds in the seventh paragraph that a hummingbird's depth of torpor on a given night depends in part on:

options.A: whether the bird has already entered torpor earlier in the week.
options.B: how many other birds share the same roost.
options.C: how much energy the bird has stored when it goes to roost.
options.D: the elevation at which the bird was raised.

5.stem: According to Passage B, the narrator "tried to be furniture" because:

options.A: he preferred reading at the counter to any conversation with customers.
options.B: the regulars wanted recognition without conversation.
options.C: most customers were too absorbed in their laundry to notice him.
options.D: his uncle had run the business that way and he saw no reason to change it.

6.stem: The passage's central claim about torpor in high-Andean hummingbirds is that torpor:

options.A: allows the birds to escape predators during the coldest hours of the night.
options.B: is a nightly strategy adjusted to conditions, not a fixed trait of a species.
options.C: is unrelated to the temperature of the site where a bird chooses to spend the night.
options.D: is shallow in most species and deep only in the largest and heaviest.

7.stem: It can reasonably be inferred from the passage that a field biologist who recorded hatchlings emerging 65 days after a clutch was laid would most likely conclude that the nest had:

options.A: been shaded by conservation workers.
options.B: reached temperatures above 33 degrees.
options.C: produced hatchlings that were mostly male.
options.D: been held close to the pivotal temperature.

8.stem: The drummer's remark in Passage A, "You played beautifully. You just weren't here," is best understood to mean that the author:

options.A: had been so absorbed in the music that he lost all track of his surroundings.
options.B: played skillfully but without responding to what the other musicians were doing.
options.C: played so nervously that his mistakes were obvious to every member of the band.
options.D: had chosen material that was far too difficult for a player of his age and training.

9.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: describe the life cycle of the loggerhead sea turtle from nesting through the thirty years to maturity.
options.B: argue that loggerhead clutches should be relocated to cooler, deeper stretches of beach as a matter of routine.
options.C: explain how nest temperature sets the sex of sea turtle hatchlings and why this now concerns conservationists.
options.D: compare sex determination in mammals with the temperature-dependent systems found in all reptiles.

10.stem: In Passage B, the author refers to the ancient bard and his stock epithets primarily in order to:

options.A: argue that jazz musicians should study poetry in order to improve their phrasing.
options.B: show that building fluency out of formulas is common to improvised arts in general.
options.C: suggest that oral epic was a more demanding art form than jazz improvisation.
options.D: demonstrate that formulas were once acceptable but are no longer artistically valid.

11.stem: It can reasonably be inferred from the passage that a tax abatement offered to a regional chain usually fails to attract a store because:

options.A: the abatement does nothing to increase the number of customers the store would serve.
options.B: regional chains prefer to build their own stores rather than lease existing ones.
options.C: discount chains typically outbid regional grocers for the same sites.
options.D: residents object to public money being spent on a private business.

12.stem: The passage as a whole is primarily concerned with:

options.A: arguing that cities should stop planting trees and invest instead in reflective roofing and permeable pavement.
options.B: demonstrating that proximity to water is the most important influence on how hot a neighborhood becomes.
options.C: describing the method researchers used to measure surface temperatures in five neighborhoods of one city.
options.D: explaining why heat concentrates in some neighborhoods and what that implies for how cities respond.

13.stem: According to the passage, cities cool little after dark because:

options.A: trees stop transpiring after sunset and so no longer cool the air.
options.B: the air trapped in urban canyons cannot circulate once the wind drops at night.
options.C: buildings continue to generate heat from lighting and air conditioning through the night.
options.D: pavement and masonry release the heat they absorbed during the day slowly, over many hours.

14.stem: According to the passage, the sex of a sea turtle embryo is set:

options.A: during a window in the middle third of the incubation period.
options.B: when the female selects a site and digs the nest chamber.
options.C: in the final days before the hatchlings emerge from the sand.
options.D: at the moment of fertilization, by inherited chromosomes.

15.stem: According to Passage A, the library's internal audit found that overdue fines:

options.A: produced about one percent of revenue and took a similar share of staff time.
options.B: had lowered the proportion of items eventually returned from 96 to 95 percent.
options.C: were concentrated in the two branches that served the city's wealthiest neighborhoods.
options.D: were the library system's largest single source of unrestricted operating income.

16.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that a street newly planted with saplings would:

options.A: cool the neighborhood more effectively than preserving a single mature tree would.
options.B: provide little cooling for many years, since its shade depends on a mature canopy.
options.C: raise the share of impervious surface in the neighborhood where the saplings are planted.
options.D: lower surface temperatures by fifteen to twenty degrees within the first summer after planting.

17.stem: The central claim of the passage is that:

options.A: automatic enrollment in retirement plans is the single most effective policy tool yet found for changing behavior.
options.B: public-health campaigns have succeeded because they change what people want, which in turn changes what they do.
options.C: people who fail to keep their resolutions usually lack the self-discipline that successful people have.
options.D: whether a new behavior lasts depends less on the strength of the intention behind it than on the conditions around it.

18.stem: According to the passage, which of the following turned out to be a strong predictor of whether a new recreation-center member was still attending at week twelve?

options.A: How much the member had paid for the membership at the start of the term
options.B: How motivated the member reported being when signing up for the membership
options.C: How many visits the member made to the center during the first week
options.D: Whether the member came at a regular time on regular days

19.stem: According to the passage, the studios began commissioning original scores in the mid-1920s in response to:

options.A: the commercial arrival of synchronized sound in American theaters.
options.B: demands from the musicians' unions for steadier work in the palaces.
options.C: complaints that accompanists played inappropriate or repetitive music.
options.D: the rising cost of the photoplay music anthologies for small theaters.

20.stem: The main idea of Passage A is that:

options.A: genuine improvisation lies in responding to the other musicians, not in how much material a player has learned.
options.B: audiences are better judges of whether a performance was truly improvised than the musicians on the stand are.
options.C: a musician who memorizes recorded solos note for note will never become a competent improviser.
options.D: the fear of performing in public fades naturally once a musician has accumulated enough years of experience.

21.stem: According to the passage, a cue sheet was:

options.A: a list of scene descriptions paired with suggested pieces, sent out by the distributor.
options.B: a set of instructions from a local censor specifying which scenes were to be shortened.
options.C: an original score commissioned by a studio for one of its most expensive productions.
options.D: an anthology of short pieces organized by dramatic situation rather than by composer.

22.stem: According to Passage B, surveys of nonusers in the low-income neighborhoods ranked fines:

options.A: as a concern raised mainly by the parents of young children in those neighborhoods.
options.B: as the most common reason that residents gave for letting a library card lapse.
options.C: below transportation, hours, and lack of awareness as reasons for not visiting.
options.D: higher after the fines were abolished than they had before the policy change.

23.stem: It can reasonably be inferred from the passage that the second kitchen chair was moved to the landing because:

options.A: Lena's mother intended to take it back to her own household that summer.
options.B: the apartment above the shop was too small for two chairs at the table.
options.C: it had been damaged and was waiting for the grandfather to find time to repair it.
options.D: the grandfather did not want a daily reminder of his recently deceased wife.

24.stem: The passage suggests that when a town's grocery store closes, the pharmacy, hardware store, and diner tend to close as well because:

options.A: the grocery store generated the daily trips that carried customers past them.
options.B: most residents leave the town within a decade of the closure.
options.C: the discount store that replaces the grocer also sells pharmacy and hardware goods.
options.D: the wholesaler that served the grocer also served the town's other businesses.

25.stem: The detail that the brass tweezers "lay untouched beside the lamp for the rest of the afternoon" most strongly suggests that the grandfather asked for them in order to:

options.A: give himself a moment to recover without appearing to need one.
options.B: test whether Lena had learned the names of the tools.
options.C: replace a pair of tweezers that had become too worn to use safely.
options.D: signal that he wanted her to stop sweeping near the bench.

26.stem: Passage A suggests that children in low-income households stopped visiting the library primarily because:

options.A: they had accumulated overdue fines of their own on borrowed children's books.
options.B: their schools had stopped running the library's card registration drives.
options.C: their cards were tied to their parents' accounts, which had been blocked.
options.D: the branches nearest to their homes had shortened their weekday hours.

27.stem: According to the passage, Lena rearranged the workbench:

options.A: early in the morning, before her grandfather had come down to the shop.
options.B: after her grandfather asked her to move the lamp closer to the vise.
options.C: while her grandfather was busy helping a customer at the counter.
options.D: on the same day she first saw his hand tremble over the watch.

28.stem: The passage as a whole can best be described as:

options.A: a technical history of the veranda in colonial architecture and its later adaptations.
options.B: an argument that air conditioning did lasting harm to the social life of American towns.
options.C: a defense of the planned communities that now require houses to have porches of a specified depth.
options.D: an account of the porch's rise, decline, and partial return, framed by one historian's view.

29.stem: The main purpose of Passage B is to:

options.A: propose that the library extend its branch hours and improve bus service to its poorest neighborhoods.
options.B: argue that the evidence credited to the fine-free policy is weaker than its advocates claim.
options.C: show that the river city's registration gains were caused by its expansion of digital lending.
options.D: defend daily overdue fines as the most effective way to ensure that borrowed books are returned.

30.stem: The passage indicates that small-format discount chains can operate profitably in towns where a supermarket cannot because they:

options.A: receive tax abatements from the towns they enter.
options.B: own their buildings outright rather than leasing them.
options.C: occupy small buildings, employ few people, and stock mainly nonperishable goods.
options.D: are financed by local sales-tax revenue.

31.stem: According to the passage, researchers once believed that hummingbird torpor stopped at a floor in the high teens or low twenties Celsius because:

options.A: they assumed some vital process would fail below that temperature.
options.B: the temperature probes then available could not register lower values.
options.C: captive birds never cooled beyond that point.
options.D: no species had ever been observed overnight at its own roost site.

32.stem: According to the passage, Osei believes that when a resolution fails, the usual reason is that the person:

options.A: chose a goal that was too ambitious to be realistic in the first place.
options.B: attempted the change at a time of year that offered no fresh start.
options.C: lacked the self-discipline that carrying out the change would require.
options.D: changed the behavior without changing the environment around it.

33.stem: The passage indicates that Species E cooled and saved the least because:

options.A: its heart cannot slow as far as the hearts of smaller birds can.
options.B: it roosts in cavities where the surrounding air stays warmer.
options.C: it had been fed to satiation before going to roost.
options.D: its larger body loses heat more slowly, so it has less to gain from torpor.

34.stem: Based on the passage, the author would most likely agree that the cafeteria water-dispenser experiment shows that:

options.A: signs and price changes are the most effective tools for changing behavior in shared workplaces.
options.B: people will choose water over other drinks whenever it is offered to them free of charge.
options.C: the employees in the experiment had been unaware before the move that water was available at all.
options.D: changing how convenient a behavior is alters what people do without altering what they prefer.

35.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Silent film accompanists were largely untrained musicians whose failings forced the studios to take control of film music away from the theaters.
options.B: The commercial arrival of synchronized sound in 1927 was the most disruptive technological change in the history of American cinema and its music.
options.C: Composed scores distributed by the studios steadily improved the music heard with silent films until synchronized sound made such scores unnecessary.
options.D: Live accompaniment for silent films was a distinct improvised art shaped by its audience, and it is hard to recover because it was never recorded.

36.stem: According to the passage, the porch's architectural ancestors served which of the following practical purposes?

options.A: displaying furniture such as swings, rockers, and wicker chairs.
options.B: keeping sun off walls and keeping floodwater away from entries.
options.C: allowing a house and its occupants to be seen clearly from the street.
options.D: providing a sheltered place for guests to sleep in hot weather.

37.stem: Which of the following statements best describes the passage as a whole?

options.A: A teenager who resents a summer job arranged by her mother discovers, over several weeks, an unexpected talent for repairing antique watches.
options.B: A granddaughter notices her grandfather's failing hands and eyes and finds ways to help him that neither of them has to acknowledge.
options.C: An aging craftsman, grieving his wife, decides to close the business they ran together and hands its remaining customers over to his granddaughter.
options.D: A mother and daughter quietly disagree about who should take responsibility for an elderly relative who refuses to leave the shop he has run for decades.

38.stem: In Passage A, the narrator says the laundromat was "the only place I ever saw him sit still." The passage most strongly suggests this was because:

options.A: he wanted to model patience for his daughter while she did her homework.
options.B: carrying the laundry down three flights of stairs left him too tired to do anything else.
options.C: the orange plastic chair by the window was more comfortable than any seat he had at home.
options.D: at the laundromat the machines did the work, leaving him nothing to fix or attend to.

39.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to:

options.A: demonstrate that rural depopulation cannot be reversed by local policy.
options.B: argue that small-format discount chains should be barred from entering rural markets.
options.C: explain why rural grocery stores close and examine how towns have responded.
options.D: describe the daily operations of a municipally owned grocery store in a small town.

40.stem: According to the passage, Walter replaced the bell above the door because:

options.A: Corinne had complained about the sound of the old one.
options.B: the old one had cracked and sounded worse each year.
options.C: the building was about to be demolished for condominiums.
options.D: a new one was needed to draw customers to the shop.

41.stem: It can reasonably be inferred that the critics of the porch revival mentioned in the seventh paragraph believe that:

options.A: building porches will not by itself produce the street life that filled them.
options.B: the porches in planned communities are too shallow to be used comfortably.
options.C: the garage door is a more honest architectural statement than the porch ever was.
options.D: children raised near porches will eventually use them as their grandparents did.

42.stem: Which of the following best describes what happens in the passage as a whole?

options.A: Two people long apart approach each other indirectly, through familiar objects and routines rather than open conversation.
options.B: Two old business partners argue over whether a shop should be modernized and finally agree to divide the responsibility for it.
options.C: A woman tries to persuade the owner of a failing repair shop to sell the building before the town replaces it with condominiums.
options.D: A customer visits a clockmaker's shop to have an heirloom repaired and ends up discussing a proposed development on the waterfront.

43.stem: In the final paragraph, Walter's telling Corinne "Then you can lock up" is best understood as:

options.A: an indirect way of trusting her with the shop and asking her to stay.
options.B: an admission that he can no longer manage the shop's closing routine by himself.
options.C: a reminder that the shop closes at five and that she should not plan to linger.
options.D: a hint that he would rather be left alone with the carriage clock he is repairing.

44.stem: According to the passage, a torpid hummingbird rewarms itself in the morning by:

options.A: moving to a sunlit branch.
options.B: feeding on nectar.
options.C: increasing the rate of its breathing.
options.D: shivering.

45.stem: The passage identifies all of the following as contributing to the porch's decline EXCEPT:

options.A: the rise of planned communities.
options.B: the spread of air conditioning.
options.C: the arrival of television.
options.D: the dominance of the automobile.

46.stem: According to the passage, why are people who take up a new behavior shortly after moving more likely to keep it?

options.A: People tend to feel more motivated when their surroundings are unfamiliar.
options.B: New cities generally offer better facilities for the behavior than the ones people left.
options.C: The new behavior is not competing with an old routine that the surroundings keep triggering.
options.D: A move usually leaves people with more free time in which to practice the new behavior.

47.stem: According to the passage, the independent grocers most likely to have survived the period from 1990 to 2015 were those that:

options.A: owned their buildings and paid themselves very little.
options.B: relocated to regional centers where sales volume was higher.
options.C: converted to a small-format discount model with fewer employees.
options.D: negotiated smaller minimum orders with their wholesalers.

48.stem: According to the passage, evaporation from a lawn lowers temperature because:

options.A: the water vapor forms a layer that reflects sunlight back toward the sky.
options.B: moist soil beneath the grass absorbs considerably less sunlight than dry soil does.
options.C: energy spent turning water into vapor is energy that would otherwise have become heat.
options.D: the blades of grass shade the ground beneath them from direct sunlight.

49.stem: According to the passage, a sea turtle population can tolerate a female-skewed sex ratio for a time because:

options.A: a single male can fertilize the eggs of a large number of females.
options.B: the skew reverses on its own once the beaches cool in winter.
options.C: warmer nests also produce larger and hardier hatchlings.
options.D: females emerging from warm nests mature more quickly.

50.stem: It can reasonably be inferred that the studios' composed scores "traveled poorly to everywhere else" because most theaters outside the palaces:

options.A: lacked the orchestras and rehearsal time that the distributed scores assumed.
options.B: had their scores removed by local censors along with the scenes that were cut.
options.C: preferred the photoplay anthologies to any score that arrived with the print.
options.D: were refused prints of the most expensive productions by the distributors.

51.stem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that Corinne and Walter are:

options.A: a daughter and her father who have not seen each other since she left home.
options.B: a longtime customer and the shopkeeper she has bought clocks from for years.
options.C: former business partners who fell out over how to run the shop.
options.D: a reporter and a shop owner she is interviewing about a development plan.
